performers: Louis Krasner, violin; The Cleveland Orchestra; Artur Rodzinski
intro: Louis Krasner, who commissioned Berg’s Violin Concerto and played its first performance, recorded the second movement with the Cleveland Orchestra under Artur Rodzinski on 15 December 1940. It runs from a violent Allegro, through a cadenza and an orchestral climax, to variations on the chorale Es ist genug.

sections.label: A · Allegro, violent opening and dotted rhythms
B · Cadenza and climax of the Allegro

cues.title: Opening of Part II: Allegro
cues.text: The second movement begins violently, with an intensity of dissonance Berg has so far avoided. He wanted the opening played with the freedom of a cadenza. A strictly rhythmic style, ruled by a dotted rhythm, takes over later.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: the second movement “enters violently”, with cadenza-like freedom at the opening and a strictly rhythmic style, dominated by a dotted rhythm, later on.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Krasner and the commission
cues.text: Krasner, the soloist here, suggested the concerto to Berg and played it first, in Barcelona on 19 April 1936. Webern was to have conducted but withdrew, and Hermann Scherchen took over with next to no rehearsal time.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: the commission, the première on 19 April 1936 with the Orquestra Pau Casals, Webern’s withdrawal and Scherchen’s rescue. The 1941 review states that Krasner “suggested to Berg that he compose a concerto”: The American Music Lover (later The American Record Guide), vol. 8 no. 1, September 1941, review of Columbia set M-465, pp. 17–18, https://archive.org/details/sim_american-record-guide_1941-09_8_1.

cues.title: Manon Gropius
cues.text: Berg wrote the concerto in memory of Manon Gropius, Alma Mahler’s daughter, who died of polio on 22 April 1935, aged eighteen. His title page reads “Dem Andenken eines Engels” (to the memory of an angel).
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: Manon Gropius’s death on 22 April 1935 and the inscription on the title page, “Dem Andenken eines Engels”.

cues.title: Cadenza, then the climax
cues.text: A demanding cadenza halts the forward movement for a moment. The orchestra then returns in full force and drives the music to an immense climax, which subsides before the Adagio.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: after the strictly rhythmic section, “a demanding cadenza” halts the music, the orchestra re-enters in full force and the music reaches an immense climax before the chorale.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Adagio: the chorale
cues.text: The Adagio begins with the solo violin playing the chorale Es ist genug, accompanied by bassoon and a few orchestral strings. Its first four notes are the last four of Berg’s twelve-note row, rising by whole tones.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: the violin plays the chorale “quietly” with bassoon and a few strings, and the chorale’s first four notes are the last four of Berg’s row.

cues.title: Source of the chorale
cues.text: The tune is by Johann Rudolf Ahle and the words by Franz Joachim Burmeister. Bach harmonised it in the cantata O Ewigkeit, du Donnerwort, BWV 60. Berg’s harmonisation and Bach’s alternate through the Adagio.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: the chorale comes from Cantata No. 60, with a melody by Ahle and words by Burmeister, and “Berg’s and Bach’s harmonizations alternate and subtly intersect”.

cues.title: Variations; violins join one by one
cues.text: In the variations the melody is in muted cellos and harp, and the solo violin, also muted, joins them. One orchestral violin then joins the soloist, then another, and Berg asks the soloist to lead the violins “audibly and visibly”.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: the variations begin with the melody in muted cellos and harp; the solo violin, also muted, is joined by single orchestral violins, and Berg asks the soloist to lead them “audibly and visibly”.

cues.title: Krasner on “the real cadenza”
cues.text: Krasner reported that Berg regarded this passage, with the orchestral violins joining the soloist one by one, as “the real cadenza” of the concerto.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: Louis Krasner “stated that to Berg, this was ‘the real cadenza’ of the concerto”.

cues.title: Orchestral strings drop away
cues.text: The orchestral strings drop away as gradually as they entered, until only the soloist is left.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: “The other strings drop away as gradually as they had entered until only the soloist is left.”
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Carinthian song, then the close
cues.text: The Carinthian folk song from the first movement returns, in Steinberg’s words “as if from a great distance”. The chorale, surrounded by figuration in the solo strings, then leads to the close.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: the Carinthian song is heard “as if from a great distance”, and the chorale, “garlanded about with a filigree of solo strings”, leads the work to its close.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda: open strings return
cues.text: The last music is a scarcely audible return of the preluding on open strings that began the concerto, when the soloist touched the four open strings G–D–A–E.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg, programme note on Berg’s Violin Concerto, Boston Symphony Orchestra, https://www.bso.org/works/berg-violin-concerto: “The last music we hear is a scarcely audible recollection of the preluding on open strings where it all began”; the opening is the violin’s entrance on the open strings from G up to E.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Composer of Wozzeck, an opera about an exploited soldier, and of a twelve-note concerto that quotes a Bach chorale and is dedicated to the memory of Manon Gropius.
facts: Vienna; a summer house by the Wörthersee from 1932
Violin Concerto, 1935; commissioned by Louis Krasner, dedicated to Manon Gropius
composer.background:
In 1904 Berg’s brother Charly secretly took some of Alban’s songs to Arnold Schoenberg. Their sister Smaragda had spotted an advertisement for lessons in harmony and counterpoint. Alban was nineteen, a bookseller’s son from Vienna, writing songs and working in the civil service. His father had died four years earlier, and there was little money for tuition. Schoenberg accepted him all the same, though he could not pay the fee. Recalling their first meeting in a recording made in 1949, Schoenberg described “a very tall youngster and extremely timid”, whose songs stood stylistically between Hugo Wolf and Brahms.

An inheritance in 1906 allowed Berg to leave the office. When his mother proposed the conservatoire, Schoenberg heard, he wept until she agreed he could stay with his teacher. Lessons lasted until 1910. The Piano Sonata, Op. 1, completed in 1908, shows Schoenberg’s developing variation at work: small phrases change and grow, through whole-tone passages to a final B minor. The String Quartet, Op. 3, shares its themes between two movements; its opening idea returns near the close.
